public_health_question.v: How was a human leptospirosis case in a low-incidence state linked to a canine outbreak, and did canine vaccination practices change after the public health response?

ev.q: Public health authorities investigated to determine potential sources of infection, identify additional cases, and recommend control measures.

The office of the State Animal Health Official (SAHO) obtained histories for canine leptospirosis cases, reviewed veterinary records, and interviewed veterinary clinic staff members.
a survey was distributed to veterinary clinics throughout Wyoming to assess changes in canine leptospirosis vaccination rates
WDH staff members reviewed medical records, interviewed the patient, and reviewed reportable conditions data* to monitor for additional cases.
The National Electronic Disease Surveillance System for Wyoming was used to monitor for additional cases.
Six of 10 clinics in the affected city and eight clinics in rural counties responded.

equity.level_reason: The only SPD-like contrast is rural vs affected-city veterinary clinics on canine vaccination, which describes clinic geography rather than human social position; the patient's occupation is a route of exposure.

level_alternative.reason: Rural clinics' vaccination recommendation and owner compliance are reported beside the city's, which a reader could count as group-specific results by rurality.

ev.q: Responding rural clinics reported recommending vaccination more frequently than did clinics in the affected city

notes: Single human case plus 13 canine cases; the only computed quantities are clinic-reported pre/post canine vaccination percentages from 14 responding clinics, so data_focus is limited (yes is defensible). Canine vaccination is an animal vaccine, so vaccine_outcome_type is null. The case-definition titer criteria are case confirmation, not comparisons.
